title: Imports: Reusing the Repository's Dirichlet Theorem
content: The file imports Proofs.DirichletsTheorem — the gallery's machine-checked Dirichlet theorem — together with Mathlib.Data.ZMod.Basic (for the ZMod ↔ mod cast bridge) and Mathlib.Tactic. All of the infinitude content comes from the imported dirichlet_modEq; this file adds only the per-modulus specializations and the ZMod cast lemmas. Because the entire import closure is sorry-free and axiom-free, the two infinitude theorems are genuinely verified, not conditional.
mathContext: Dependency chain: this file → Proofs.DirichletsTheorem.dirichlet_modEq → Mathlib's Nat.infinite_setOf_prime_and_modEq. ZMod.Basic supplies ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff for the cast bridges.

title: OQ-01 and the p ≡ -1 (mod q) Spectrum
content: The module docstring states the OQ-01 deliverable and presents the spectrum-coverage table for the family of residue classes p ≡ -1 (mod q). For q ∈ {3, 4, 6} the class admits a genuinely elementary, L-function-free Euclid-style proof (handled in this slug's sibling files); q = 8 is the conjectured elementary frontier; and q ∈ {12, 24} — the moduli of this file — are settled instead by specializing the full Dirichlet theorem, because their unit groups (Klein-4 for 12, (ℤ/2ℤ)³ for 24) make a single-construction Euclid argument awkward. In every (ZMod q)ˣ the residue -1 is the distinguished involution, which is why p ≡ -1 (mod q) is the canonical 'easy' class across all q.
mathContext: (ZMod 12)ˣ ≅ Klein-4 = {1, 5, 7, 11}, with 11 ≡ -1 the unique order-2 unit; (ZMod 24)ˣ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)³ = {1,5,7,11,13,17,19,23}, with 23 ≡ -1 simultaneously -1 mod 8 and -1 mod 3 under CRT 24 = 8·3.

title: ZMod ↔ mod Bridge Lemmas
content: zmod_12_eq_eleven_iff and zmod_24_eq_twentythree_iff each prove (p : ZMod q) = a ↔ p % q = a. The proof recasts the literal a as a Nat-cast so that ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff applies, turning the ZMod equality into a Nat.ModEq, which unfold + omega then settle. These bridges are what let the file present every result in both the elementary % q = a form and the ZMod-cast form without re-proving the infinitude.
mathContext: $(p : \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}) = a \iff p \bmod q = a$. Via $\mathrm{ZMod.natCast\_eq\_natCast\_iff} : (a : \mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z}) = (b : \mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z}) \iff a \equiv b\ [\mathrm{MOD}\ c]$, then $\mathrm{unfold\ Nat.ModEq};\ \mathrm{omega}$.

title: infinitely_many_primes_11_mod_12
content: The q = 12 case of OQ-01: the set of primes p with p % 12 = 11 is infinite. The proof establishes Nat.Coprime 11 12 by decide, instantiates the imported dirichlet_modEq at (a, q) = (11, 12), then converts the resulting set {p | p ≡ 11 [MOD 12]} to {p | p % 12 = 11} — the two differ only by unfolding Nat.ModEq, discharged by ext and simp [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Nat.ModEq].
mathContext: $\mathrm{Set.Infinite}\,\{p \mid \mathrm{Nat.Prime}\,p \wedge p \bmod 12 = 11\}$, from $\mathrm{dirichlet\_modEq}\,(12 \neq 0)\,(11 \perp 12)$. 11 is the unique order-2 element of the Klein-4 group $(\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z})^\times$.

title: infinitely_many_primes_23_mod_24
content: The q = 24 case of OQ-01: the set of primes p with p % 24 = 23 is infinite. Structurally identical to the q = 12 theorem, instantiated at (a, q) = (23, 24) with coprimality 23 ⊥ 24 by decide. Under the CRT splitting 24 = 8·3, the residue 23 is the unique unit that is simultaneously -1 (mod 8) and -1 (mod 3) in (ZMod 24)ˣ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)³.

title: ZMod-Cast Forms of Both Results
content: primes_11_mod_12_zmod_form and primes_23_mod_24_zmod_form restate the two infinitude results with the predicate (p : ZMod q) = a instead of p % q = a — the formulation that character-sum and L-function arguments consume. Each proof rewrites the set using the corresponding bridge lemma (zmod_12_eq_eleven_iff / zmod_24_eq_twentythree_iff) to reduce to the elementary theorem, then applies it directly.
mathContext: $\mathrm{Set.Infinite}\,\{p \mid \mathrm{Nat.Prime}\,p \wedge (p : \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}) = a\}$ for $(a, q) \in \{(11, 12), (23, 24)\}$, reduced via the bridge lemmas to the $\% q = a$ theorems.
